title: fix(wasm): harden allocation failure handling
body:
## Problem

The custom allocator ignored a failed `memory.grow()` and could advance heap metadata beyond the available linear memory. JavaScript then observed a later `WebAssembly.RuntimeError: memory access out of bounds` instead of an allocation failure.

The TypeScript wrapper also treated zero pointers as valid and did not release every temporary buffer when allocation, copying, a WASM call, or later cleanup failed. CTR input ownership was split between C and TypeScript.

## Change

- Return `NULL` without mutating allocator state when size arithmetic or memory growth fails.
- Convert zero pointers to `RangeError: WASM memory allocation failed` before accessing linear memory.
- Normalize wasm32 pointers and sizes, preserve cleanup on every exceptional path, and publish persistent module state only after complete initialization.
- Use validated aligned allocation for AES and libdeflate contexts, and keep CTR input and output buffers owned by TypeScript.
- Build both scalar and SIMD package artifacts from the same command.

Valid cryptographic, compression, and hashing behavior is unchanged. AES input-shape validation is separate.

## Evidence

Eleven focused cases were added. A deterministic two-page WASM fixture proves that failed growth leaves linear memory and allocator state unchanged, then verifies that released storage can still be reused. Existing scalar and SIMD stress coverage verifies stable memory use.

Two independent builds produced identical checked-in artifacts:

- scalar: `cc2d1f785688d9bdfe1c325d25c4685ab4c8fd9368b61bf5c5944467690d50b9`
- SIMD: `f7ff8baf87fbc7ae365cc3fde7345c6dba05efbabe8228d8e617462d5c1fdb4f`

The rebuilt scalar artifact is 49,336 bytes instead of 57,363; the SIMD artifact is 52,391 bytes instead of 59,241. The package build now copies the artifacts produced by the pinned Docker toolchain, where Binaryen is available and Clang runs `wasm-opt -O3` after linking. That removes a 3,284-byte name section and unreachable internal functions. Both artifacts retain the same 20 public exports as their predecessors.

The original production exception was not retained, so this fixes a real allocation defect without claiming that WASM allocation failure caused that incident.

## Scope

This does not change MTProto retry or settlement policy, transport buffering, application logging, or public AES input validation.

title: fix(core): abort requests after a flush exception
body:
> **Draft dependency:** This PR is based on #163. After #163 merges, this branch will be rebased onto upstream `master` and the PR will be marked ready for review.

## Problem

When `_doFlush()` throws, the current catch resets the MTProto session while retaining and requeueing its requests. A deterministic packet-construction or encryption error can therefore run the same path repeatedly while callers remain pending.

## Change

Treat the mutated session as failed:

- report the original error through the public `onError` chain;
- reject every queued or registered RPC owned by that session exactly once;
- clear request timers and abort hooks, and cancel the active PFS authorization attempt;
- invalidate queued idle work and stale inactivity continuations;
- preserve the transport, auth keys, time offset, and shared salts;
- do not reconnect or automatically retry failed requests.

A later new request may use a replacement MTProto session on the existing transport. Cleanup completes before `onError` is emitted, so an error listener may submit that new work.

Session-wide rejection is intentional: packet construction mutates shared message IDs, sequence numbers, chains, service queues, pending-message maps, and timers. There is no complete rollback boundary that makes only part of the old session safe to retain.

## Evidence

Nine focused cases were added for exact-once settlement, PFS cancellation and mode changes, stale idle and inactivity work, owner-safe service markers, error delivery, replacement-session bookkeeping, and absence of automatic retry. The three prerequisite ownership cases in #163 also verify settlement under this policy.

Two production CPU profiles were consistent with repeated execution through the flush/reset/requeue path. The original exception was not retained, so this PR does not identify AES-IGE or any other packet operation as the cause.

## Limitations

- Ciphertext already handed to `PersistentConnection.send()` cannot be withdrawn and may still cross the transport boundary.
- Rejected requests have no exactly-once-delivery or remote-cancellation guarantee.
- This does not identify the original packet-construction or encryption error.
- It does not change `PersistentConnection`, transport replacement, or general auth-key and shared-salt lifecycle.

title: fix(core): preserve RPC ownership during flush construction
body:
## Problem

A fresh RPC leaves `queuedRpc` before packet construction assigns its message ID and inserts it into `pendingMessages`:

```text
queuedRpc -> selected batch -> pendingMessages[msgId]
```

If packet construction throws in that interval, the existing keep-pending session reset cannot find the RPC. Its promise remains pending without a queue or pending-map owner.

## Change

`_flush()` now retains the selected batch while `_doFlush()` constructs the packet. When construction throws:

- registered RPCs remain in `pendingMessages` for the existing reset path;
- non-cancelled RPCs without a matching pending record have provisional message state cleared and return to the queue;
- the original batch order is preserved across partial registration;
- cancelled or timed-out RPCs are not restored.

The existing session reset, reconnect, error reporting, and retry policy are unchanged. An encryption exception occurs after fresh RPCs have been registered, so it does not create this ownership gap.

## Evidence

Three focused cases were added for failure before registration, failure after partial registration, and timeout reentrancy. They verify that each surviving RPC has exactly one owner, original order is preserved, and settled RPCs are not revived.

An additional temporary stress run injected every registration cutoff in a 32-RPC batch. All 1,024 selected-RPC observations remained reachable through the normal reset path.

## Scope

This PR only repairs RPC ownership during packet construction. It does not change retry limits, ciphertext buffering, PFS lifecycle, transport behavior, or flush-failure policy.

title: fix(wasm): validate public AES input lengths
body:
> **Draft dependency:** This PR is based on #162. After #162 merges, this branch will be rebased onto upstream `master` and the PR will be marked ready for review.

The smaller `mtcute.wasm` and `mtcute-simd.wasm` files currently shown in this PR are inherited from #162, whose pinned Docker build applies Binaryen optimization while retaining the same public exports. This PR's own commit does not modify either binary. Those inherited binary changes will disappear from this diff after #162 merges and this branch is rebased.

## Problem

The public AES-IGE wrappers accepted data that was not block-aligned and key or IV values that did not match their fixed shared buffers. The C loop processes complete 16-byte vectors; short shared inputs retained old bytes, while long inputs could overwrite adjacent memory. AES-CTR used the same shared buffers without validating its key or IV.

## Change

- Require AES-IGE data lengths to be multiples of 16 bytes.
- Require a 32-byte AES-256 key and 32-byte IGE IV.
- Require a 32-byte AES-CTR key and 16-byte CTR IV.
- Reject invalid inputs before allocation, shared-memory writes, or C calls.
- Preserve empty IGE input and the same validation order for encryption and decryption.

Invalid inputs now produce stable `RangeError` messages. Existing MTProto and authorization callers already provide valid lengths, so their behavior is unchanged.

## Evidence

Eighteen focused cases were added. They cover validation order, exact errors, unchanged shared memory after rejection, cleanup when a valid-shape WASM call throws, and accepted empty input in scalar and SIMD builds. Fourteen instrumented precondition cases reached allocation or changed shared memory before this fix.

## Scope

Relative to #162, this PR does not change C code, allocator behavior, WASM artifacts, crypto-provider adapters, MTProto recovery, or logging. No production evidence identifies invalid AES input as the earlier incident's trigger.

Enabling usePfs makes file downloading much slower
body:
Hi! When I turn on network.usePfs, file downloading becomes much slower. Is this a desired behavior? What's the reason? 

Without pfs

=== Benchmark Results ===
Successful downloads (fastest to slowest):
1. downloadAsNodeStream: 2787ms
2. downloadToFile: 3081ms (+294ms)
3. downloadAsIterable: 3294ms (+507ms)
4. downloadAsStream: 3391ms (+604ms)
5. downloadAsBuffer: 3449ms (+662ms)

Fastest method: downloadAsNodeStream (19.2% faster than slowest)
=== End Benchmark ===

With pfs

=== Benchmark Results ===
Successful downloads (fastest to slowest):
1. downloadAsStream: 8601ms
2. downloadAsNodeStream: 9192ms (+591ms)
3. downloadAsIterable: 9346ms (+745ms)
4. downloadAsBuffer: 9573ms (+972ms)
5. downloadToFile: 11108ms (+2507ms)

Fastest method: downloadAsStream (22.6% faster than slowest)
=== End Benchmark ===



Is there a core limitation of the pfs method or is there a slow cryptography that can be accelerated? Thanks
